name: Lindwurm
body:
Lindwurm
CR 9

This savage beast looks like a cross between a primal snake and a primitive dragon, its long, coiling body muscular, covered in rough, green scales and supported by two arms.

XP 6,400
N Huge dragon
Init +1; Senses darkvision 60 ft., low-light vision; Perception +14

DEFENSE

AC 23, touch 9, flat-footed 22 (+1 Dex, +14 natural, –2 size)
hp 135 (10d12+70)
Fort +13, Ref +8, Will +8
Defensive Abilities corrosive blood; Immune acid, paralysis, sleep

OFFENSE

Speed 20 ft.
Melee bite +18 (2d6+9/19-20 plus grab), tail slap +17 (2d6+13)
Space 15 ft.; Reach 10 ft.
Special Attacks powerful tail, swallow whole (2d6+9 bludgeoning damage plus 4d6 acid damage, AC 17, 13 hp)

STATISTICS

Str 29, Dex 13, Con 22, Int 3, Wis 12, Cha 8
Base Atk +10; CMB +21 (+25 grapple); CMD 32 (can’t be tripped)
Feats Improved Critical (Bite), Power Attack, Toughness, Vital Strike, Weapon Focus (Bite)
Skills Perception +14, Survival +14
Languages Draconic (can’t speak)

SPECIAL ABILITIES

Corrosive Blood (Ex)

A lindwurm’s blood can corrode metal on contact. If a creature damages a lindwurm with a piercing or slashing weapon made of metal, the creature’s blood deals 4d6 points of acid damage to the metal weapon (unlike most forms of energy damage, this damage is not halved when applied to a metal object, although it does still have to penetrate the metal’s hardness). The weapon’s wielder can halve the damage the weapon takes by making a successful DC 22 Reflex save. Creatures made of metal that deal slashing or piercing damage to a lindwurm with a natural attack take 4d6 points of acid damage (a DC 22 Reflex save halves this damage). The corrosive elements of the blood fade 1 hour after it leaves the lindwurm’s body or the lindwurm dies. The save DC is Constitution-based.

Powerful Tail (Ex)

A lindwurm’s tail slap is considered a primary natural attack and adds 1-1/2 times the lindwurm’s Strength bonus to damage.

ECOLOGY

Environment temperate forests
Organization solitary, pair, or nest (3-5)
Treasure double

Many scholars are troubled by lindwurms, their heritage decidedly draconic, but without many traits common to this noble race. Most consider them much closer to linnorms than true dragons, hence the name. And indeed, a lindwurm seems to be to a linnorm what a wyvern is to a dragon. Possessed of lesser intelligence, size and magical abilities than their stronger kin, lindwurms are nevertheless dangerous and savage combatants, easily able to slaughter a whole village if enraged. Many a selfcalled dragonslayer met his end hunting a lindwurm, having his blade melted by the acidic blood and armor smashed by the beast’s tail.

Lindwurms are simple creatures, barely above animals in intellect, and spend much of their time lying about in bushes or in the sun, conserving their energy. They rarely have natural predators, and so regard most creatures with indifferent curiosity, except when hunger draws them to attack. Physically and mentally slow, a lindwurm is not stealthy or fast enough to hunt elusive prey, and so most often hunts by raiding lairs of other creatures, thus making its victims unable to escape. In the wilds, bears and other cave-dwelling animals are their most likely prey. When near civilization, lindwurms often get enticed by the convenience of animal enclosures, and so a nest of lindwurms will not think twice about barreling into a remote farm to clear out a barn, often not even acknowledging the terrified farmers hiding nearby. While lindwurms can be solitary, they most often live in small groups and rarely stray from each other, which makes them all the more dangerous.

While lindwurms have little in common with their draconic cousins, they have their own way of collecting hoards of treasure. The stomach acid of a lindwurm dissolves almost everything: bone, stone and steel. It doesn’t, however, damage noble metals and gemstones. As such, the beasts often eat the prizes of which pleasant glint catches their eye to further help with digestion, the unfortunate treasures grinding about their stomach, crushing large meals to pulp. Opening a slain lindwurm will often treat its slayer to a small mound of treasure, although often bent, scratched and mangled, further made worse by traces of acid and the repugnant smell.

A typical lindwurm is 45 feet long and weighs 7,000 pounds. Its tail is almost two thirds of its whole length, incredibly muscular and capable of unusual precision in its movements. While a lindwurm has arms, they aren’t capable of very fine motor movements and most of the time just assist the beast in dragging its body around.

Lindwurm scales most often come in various shades of green, but brownish shades happen, especially closer to deserts or hills. Some individuals (about 10%) may have a few scales with an array of different colors. Such rainbow scales are worth 250 gp each and 1d4 of them can be recovered from a slain lindwurm with this genetic trait.

A lindwurm’s scaly skin is impervious to most known acids and is often used to reinforce armor or shields. The most popular method involves using it as a material component for the energy resistance (acid) enchantment, reducing its crafting cost by 2000 gp. Rumors abound of alchemical treatments that can stabilize a lindwurm’s acidic blood, which would certainly find many uses, on and out of a battlefield.
